vocab.title: Match each term to its meaning
defs: a gain you accept in exchange for a loss somewhere else
a warning or a condition attached to what you have just said
the essential point, once everything else is taken away
to protect yourself by not committing fully to a statement
to commit harder to a position instead of softening it
to explain something in full detail, leaving nothing implied
resistance or disagreement from the people you are speaking to
to give extra weight to a point you have already made
to describe the same fact in a different way so it is understood differently

items.situation: We need one owner for each site. Say it so the point lands last.
tips: What we need is one owner for each site.
What ... is ... Move the weight to the end.

items.situation: We are losing people in the first ninety days, not to pay. Isolate it.
tips: It is the first ninety days that we are losing people in, not the pay.
It is ... that ... denies every alternative at once.

items.situation: Ray says benchmarks lag. Agree with the true part in one sentence.
tips: That is a fair caveat, and it is right.
Agree first. It stops him preparing his next sentence.

items.situation: You are being asked for a list and you have one item. Announce it.
tips: The one thing I would change is the shift pattern.
The one thing ... is ... stops the room waiting for item two.

items.situation: The argument has gone long. Reduce it to the claim.
tips: All I am saying is that money is not the driver here.
All I am saying is ... is a rescue, not a retreat.

items.situation: Close the ask in one sentence, with no hedging.
tips: In a nutshell, give me one quarter and one person.
Say the last word and stop.

listenings.text: Almost everybody who comes to me thinks the problem is their voice. It is not their voice. It is the order of the sentence. Here is what a nervous speaker does. They put every condition first, and by the time the point arrives, forty seconds have gone and nobody knows what they are being asked. Given the constraints and the timeline and the feedback from the sites, we might possibly consider looking at onboarding. What a confident speaker does is the reverse. What I need is one owner for onboarding. Then, and only then, the conditions. Same information, same words, different order, completely different room. And the second thing I fix is the ending. Do not trail off. Do not add so, yeah, at the end. Say the last word and then close your mouth. The silence is not awkward, the silence is the point landing.

I have been talked out of a position exactly twice in fifteen years, and both times it was done the same way. The person agreed with my objection first. Not politely, actually agreed, and said which part of it was right. That did something to me. I stopped preparing my next sentence and started listening, because I was no longer being resisted. Then she said, here is the part where I still think you are wrong, and gave me one fact. One. Not five. And the fact was checkable, which meant I could not argue with it without going and looking, and I was not going to go and look in front of eight people. The third thing she did was tell me what she wanted before I had to ask. People think winning an argument is about pressure. It is about removing every reason the other person has to keep defending themselves.
